articles.title: How Generations of Coastal Families Learned to Use Every Part of the Coconut Plant
articles.description: "1 Plant, 100 Uses" explores the many ways familiar Indian plants, leaves, fruits and trees have been part of everyday life — from food and farming to homes, traditions and natural remedies. Each story takes one plant and uncovers the surprising ways people have found it useful, often across generations. For generations, the coconut palm has been part of everyday life along India’s coast. The tree stands beside homes, along fields and near backwaters, giving something useful at almost every stage of its life. The tender coconut is opened for its water . The mature fruit is used in curries, chutneys, and sweets. Its kernel is dried or pressed for oil. The husk becomes coir. The hard shell can become fuel, charcoal, or a bowl. Leaves are woven into baskets and used for thatching. An old trunk can find its way into furniture or farm structures. For communities that have lived with coconut palms for generations, the question was rarely what to throw away. It was what could be done with what remained. The Coconut Development Board itself lists an extraordinary range of uses for the tree, including food, oil, thatching, baskets, mats, rope, furniture, charcoal, brooms, fans, containers and household implements. That is how the coconut earned its old name, ‘Kalpavriksha’, the tree of abundance. It begins with the fruit A coconut has more than one use. A young coconut is valued for its water. As it matures, the soft kernel becomes firm and develops into the white flesh used in cooking. The Coconut Development Board notes that coconuts are harvested at different stages depending on how they are going to be used. The tree stands beside homes, along fields and near backwaters, giving something useful at almost every stage of its life. Photograph: (Britannica) In coastal kitchens, the mature kernel is grated into curries and chutneys, made into coconut milk or dried to produce copra. The kernel is also pressed for coconut oil, which has long been used in cooking as well as in soaps, cosmetics and hair oils. One fruit can therefore serve several purposes before anything is left behind. And even then, the useful parts are not finished. The husk becomes coir The thick husk surrounding the coconut is one of the best examples of this way of thinking. It contains a strong natural fibre called coir. Traditionally, coconut husks were soaked in water for months before being beaten and processed by hand to separate the fibres. The fibres were then cleaned, dried and spun into yarn. That yarn became ropes, mats, brushes, brooms, mattresses and other household products. The tradition is particularly strong along the Kerala coast. India’s coir industry grew in these coastal regions and became an important source of rural employment. A Government of India release notes that coir has historically provided livelihoods to lakhs of rural artisans. The same fibre now has newer uses too. Coir mats and other products are used in gardening, while coir-based geotextiles are used for erosion control. What is left after the fibre is taken out There is still something useful after the long fibres have been removed. Coir pith is the soft, spongy material that holds the fibres together inside the husk. For years it was treated as a waste product. It is now widely used in horticulture because it holds moisture well and can be used as a soil conditioner and growing medium. In coconut gardens, husks can also be placed around the base of palms as mulch. They help retain moisture in the soil. So even the material left behind after making rope can return to the farm. The Coconut Development Board itself lists an extraordinary range of uses for the tree. Photograph: (Image generated by AI) The shell does not go straight into the bin Break open a mature coconut and the hard shell remains. Traditionally, shells have been used in simple household ways, including as containers, ladles, and fuel. Artisans have also turned them into decorative and utility objects. There are larger industries built around the same material. Coconut shells can be processed into shell powder and charcoal. Shell charcoal is also used to produce activated carbon, which has applications in water and air purification. The Ministry of Environment and Forests has documented these uses and the growing value of coconut shell products. A part of the coconut that once ended up in the fire can therefore become an industrial material. The leaves become part of the home The long green fronds are another familiar sight around coconut-growing villages. Coconut leaves have traditionally been used for roofing and thatching. Leaflets can be woven into baskets and other household articles. In many places, these skills were passed from one generation to the next. A fallen leaf was not garden waste. It was material that could be cut, dried, split, and woven. Even the old palm has value Eventually, a coconut palm becomes old, and its productive life comes to an end. The trunk can still be useful. Coconut wood has been used for rafters, beams, purlins and other components in rural buildings. It can also be made into furniture and other wood products. The Coir Board notes that coconut wood is particularly suitable for rural houses, farm buildings, sheds and similar structures. The palm that spent years producing coconuts can therefore remain useful after it has stopped doing so. The tree gives back to the soil Not everything from a coconut garden has to become a finished product. Leaves, fronds and other palm residues can be allowed to decompose or converted into manure. Research published by the Coconut Development Board describes the use of coconut garden residues as organic manure . This matters because a coconut plantation produces a steady stream of organic material. Some of it feeds people. Some becomes a household product. Some becomes an income . And some goes back into the soil. A livelihood built around leftovers Perhaps the most interesting part of the coconut story is that many of its so-called leftovers became livelihoods. The coir industry is one example. Husk that might have been discarded became fibre, yarn, mats, ropes and other products. The shell became another raw material. Coconut wood created another use for an ageing palm. The Government of India has described coir as one of India’s traditional rural industries, with its roots in the coastal states of the south. The Coconut Development Board notes that coconuts are harvested at different stages depending on how they are going to be used. Photograph: (A-Z Animals) The value is not only in the coconut that reaches the market. It is also in everything around it. A different way of looking at waste The coconut palm offers a simple idea that is easy to understand. Waste is often a matter of perspective. A husk is waste if you have no use for it. It is coir if you know how to work with it. Coir pith is waste if it is dumped. It is a growing medium if it is taken back to a garden. A shell is waste when it is discarded. It becomes fuel, charcoal, or a useful object when someone sees value in it. An old trunk is waste if it is left to rot. It becomes timber when there is a reason and a skill to use it. This knowledge did not begin with the language of sustainability. It came from living close to the land and making the most of what was available. That may be the most enduring lesson of the coconut palm . Not that one tree has a hundred uses in the same way everywhere, but that generations of coastal communities learnt to look at the whole tree rather than just the part they needed. The fruit was never just a fruit. In coastal kitchens, the mature kernel is grated into curries and chutneys. Photograph: (Paper & Tea) The husk was never just a husk. And the things left behind were rarely the end of the story.

articles.title: Delhi CM Flags Execution Delays In Infrastructure Projects, Directs Departments To Expedite Work
articles.description: Delhi CM Flags Execution Delays In Infrastructure Projects, Directs Departments To Expedite Work New Delhi, Aug 21 (KNN) Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta in a recent meeting pulled up various government departments over delays in executing key projects, including the construction of flats for judicial officers and electric bus charging infrastructure in Dwarka, officials said. The departments were directed to expedite the work, they added. The meeting reviewed the progress of major projects approved by the Finance Department’s Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) last year. Judicial Housing, E-Bus Infrastructure A Rs 171.58-crore residential complex for judicial officers in Dwarka Sector 19 was among the projects reviewed. The officials noted, “A Project Man­age­ment Con­sult­ant (PMC) has been appoin­ted by the Law depart­ment to final­ise the tender doc­u­ment, but the work has not yet been awar­ded. The project was approved in April 2025. The CM dir­ec­ted the depart­ment to take imme­di­ate action against the PMC,” The Indian Express reported. The project will comprise a multi-storey tower with 52 Type-V and 34 Type-VI quarters, along with two basements. It follows the demolition of 70 flats earlier constructed at the site after flaws were found in the buildings. Gupta also reviewed the Rs 107.02-crore power infrastructure project for charging electric buses at Cluster Depots-I and II, ISBT in Dwarka Sector 22 and the DTC depot in Sector 8. Tender documents are being finalised, officials said. Sewage and Prison Projects The CM reviewed the Rs 3,104-crore sewage infrastructure project, covering 27 decentralised sewage treatment plants (STPs), a terminal sewage pumping station and a 10-MGD STP at Delhi Gate. The project is aimed at providing sewer connections to unauthorised colonies and supporting efforts to clean the Yamuna. Work has been awarded for 11 of the 27 decentralised STPs, while tenders for 15 have been received and are to be placed before the Delhi Jal Board. Tenders have also been invited for the remaining project. The Delhi Gate STP proposal has been submitted to the National Mission for Clean Ganga for approval. A Rs 148.58-crore high-security prison in Narela, approved last year, is expected to be completed by November 2027, according to officials. Other projects reviewed included road strengthening works, drains and roads along the Najafgarh drain, a medical college at IGI Hospital and a sports hostel in Pitampura. The review comes as the Delhi government seeks to accelerate execution of major infrastructure projects and address delays in projects already approved for funding. (KNN Bureau)

articles.title: Karnataka Congress Govt under fire as Rs 104 crore shoe-sock fund stays unreleased, lakhs of students wait
articles.description: Bengaluru: The Karnataka government has approved Rs 104 crore to provide shoes and socks to students in government schools during the 2026-27 academic year, but it has yet to release the full amount, even as the supply deadline has already passed. According to a report submitted by the School Education and Literacy Department, work orders covering 36,61,267 pairs of shoes and socks had been issued as of August 10. Of these, 21,92,529 had been distributed, while 12,59,298 were still in transit. Another 2,09,440 units were under production and were expected to be delivered by August 21. As per the tender conditions, the supply process was supposed to be completed by July 31. Distribution based on the number of students and their foot measurements was expected to continue until August 15. Department Commissioner Vikas Kishore Suralkar has reportedly informed the government that the delay was partly due to the admission process, which continued until July 31, and the need to collect students’ measurements. He also warned that the government could initiate action under the Karnataka Transparency in Public Procurements Act if suppliers failed to complete the process within the stipulated period. Under the Vidya Vikas scheme, the government has decided to provide one pair of quality shoes and two pairs of socks to students from Classes 1 to 10 in government schools. The state has 36,56,613 students in these classes. However, delays in releasing funds have reportedly created difficulties for schools. In some institutions, only 20 per cent or 40 per cent of the sanctioned amount has reportedly been transferred to School Development and Monitoring Committee accounts. A headmaster said schools were reluctant to purchase shoes and socks for only a section of students with the limited amount available. “If we provide shoes and socks to only some students with the money received, it will create discrimination. We can purchase them only after receiving the full allocation. Therefore, the amount sanctioned by the government is lying in the bank account,” the headmaster said. The issue has also revived concerns over the allocation made for the scheme in recent years. The government had earmarked Rs 132 crore in 2022-23, Rs 125 crore in 2023-24, Rs 125 crore in 2024-25 and Rs 111.88 crore in 2025-26. Of the 2025-26 allocation, Rs 13.20 crore was reportedly still pending for release, according to information provided by School Education Minister Madhu Bangarappa in the legislature. Teachers have also raised concerns over the rates fixed for purchasing footwear. In previous years, the government fixed rates of Rs 265 per student for Classes 1 to 5, Rs 295 for Classes 6 to 8, and Rs 325 for Classes 9 and 10. Teachers argue that these rates have not kept pace with market prices. The cost of branded footwear has increased considerably over the years due to rising input and transportation costs. Government orders have also encouraged schools to purchase good-quality footwear, including products from reputed companies, while allowing additional contributions from donors and private organisations. Also Read: CCPA fines Amazon Rs 1 lakh for selling ordinary sweets as ‘Shri Ram Mandir Ayodhya Prasad’ without authorisation “This is the same rate that was fixed several years ago, but prices in the market have increased substantially. Fuel prices and the cost of raw materials have also gone up. The government should revise the old rates according to current market prices instead of expecting teachers to seek additional money from donors and private organisations,” another headmaster said. The government had earmarked Rs 129.84 crore in 2017-18 for shoes and socks for students from Classes 1 to 10. The same rates were subsequently continued in later years despite changes in market prices. Teachers have pointed out that a quality pair of shoes can cost significantly more than what the scheme provides. This has reportedly forced some schools to approach charitable organisations and donors to bridge the gap. Meanwhile, the department said the distribution process is progressing and that the remaining shoes and socks are expected to reach schools shortly.
